claim: Townes-Brocks Syndrome (TBS1 [MIM: 107480]) is an autosomal dominant genetic disease caused by mutations in a transcription factor called SALL1.
source: Townes-Brocks Syndrome (TBS1 [MIM: 107480]) is an autosomal dominant genetic disease, caused by mutations in a transcription factor called SALL1, characterized by the presence of imperforate anus, dysplastic ears, thumb malformations and often renal and heart impairment, among other symptoms (Botzenhart et al., 2007; Kohlhase et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to Botzenhart et al., 2007 and Kohlhase et al., 1998.

claim: TBS is characterized by the presence of imperforate anus, dysplastic ears, thumb malformations and often renal and heart impairment.
source: Townes-Brocks Syndrome (TBS1 [MIM: 107480]) is an autosomal dominant genetic disease, caused by mutations in a transcription factor called SALL1, characterized by the presence of imperforate anus, dysplastic ears, thumb malformations and often renal and heart impairment, among other symptoms (Botzenhart et al., 2007; Kohlhase et al., 1998).
evidence: The clinical features of TBS are explicitly listed and supported by citations.

claim: Some TBS features overlap those in the ciliopathic spectrum.
source: Some of these features overlap those in the ciliopathic spectrum.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the text drawing a connection between TBS and ciliopathies.

claim: Primary cilia defects are contributing factors to TBS etiology.
source: It has been recently demonstrated that primary cilia defects are contributing factors to TBS etiology (Bozal-Basterra et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by a citation to Bozal-Basterra et al., 2018.

claim: Truncated SALL1, either by itself or in complex with full length protein (SALL1FL), can interact with CCP110 and CEP97.
source: Truncated SALL1, either by itself or in complex with full length protein (SALL1FL), can interact with CCP110 and CEP97.
evidence: This is a direct statement about protein interactions.

claim: Truncated SALL1 interaction with CCP110 and CEP97 results in reduction of these negative regulators at the mother centriole and promotes ciliogenesis.
source: As a consequence, those negative regulators are reduced at the mother centriole (MC) and ciliogenesis is promoted (Bozal-Basterra et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated and supported by citation to Bozal-Basterra et al., 2018.

claim: Primary cilia are sensory organelles that have a crucial role in cell signaling and protein trafficking during development and organ homeostasis.
source: Primary cilia are sensory organelles that have a crucial role in cell signaling and protein trafficking during development and organ homeostasis.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the function of primary cilia, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: The Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) pathway is the best characterized pathway influenced by cilia function.
source: Although several key pathways are influenced by cilia function (Wnt, TGFbeta, PDGFRalpha, Notch), the best characterized is the Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) pathway (Goetz and Anderson, 2010).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citation to Goetz and Anderson, 2010.

claim: Shh binds to its receptor PTCH1 and leads to ciliary enrichment of the transmembrane protein Smoothened (SMO).
source: Briefly, Shh binds to its receptor PTCH1 and leads to ciliary enrichment of the transmembrane protein Smoothened (SMO), with concomitant conversion of the transcription factor GLI3 from a cleaved repressor to a full-length activator form, leading to activation of Shh target genes.
evidence: This is a direct description of the Shh signaling mechanism.

claim: Shh signaling leads to conversion of the transcription factor GLI3 from a cleaved repressor to a full-length activator form.
source: Briefly, Shh binds to its receptor PTCH1 and leads to ciliary enrichment of the transmembrane protein Smoothened (SMO), with concomitant conversion of the transcription factor GLI3 from a cleaved repressor to a full-length activator form, leading to activation of Shh target genes.
evidence: This is a direct description of GLI3 processing in Shh signaling.

claim: PTCH1 and GLI1 are Shh target genes.
source: Two such genes are PTCH1 and GLI1 (encoding the Shh receptor and a transcriptional activator, respectively), exemplifying the feedback and fine-tuning of the Shh pathway.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as examples of Shh target genes.

claim: Cilia arise from the centrosome, a cellular organelle composed of two barrel-shaped microtubule-based structures called the centrioles.
source: Cilia arise from the centrosome, a cellular organelle composed of two barrel-shaped microtubule-based structures called the centrioles.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the structural relationship between cilia and centrosomes.

claim: Primary cilia are nucleated from the mother centriole at the membrane-anchored basal body upon entry into the G0 phase.
source: Cilia are nucleated from the MC at the membrane-anchored basal body upon entry into the G0 phase, and they reabsorb as cells progress from G1 to S phase, completely disassembling in mitosis (Rezabkova et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citation to Rezabkova et al., 2016.

claim: Primary cilia reabsorb as cells progress from G1 to S phase, completely disassembling in mitosis.
source: Cilia are nucleated from the MC at the membrane-anchored basal body upon entry into the G0 phase, and they reabsorb as cells progress from G1 to S phase, completely disassembling in mitosis (Rezabkova et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citation to Rezabkova et al., 2016.

claim: Centrioles are surrounded by protein-based matrix, the pericentriolar material (PCM).
source: Centrioles are surrounded by protein-based matrix, the pericentriolar material (PCM) (Conduit et al., 2015; Vertii et al., 2016).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by citations to Conduit et al., 2015 and Vertii et al., 2016.

claim: In eukaryotic cells, PCM proteins are concentrically arranged around a centriole in a highly organized manner.
source: In eukaryotic cells, PCM proteins are concentrically arranged around a centriole in a highly organized manner (Fu and Glover, 2012; Lawo et al., 2012; Mennella et al., 2012; Sonnen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Proper positioning and organization of PCM proteins may be important for promoting different cellular processes in a spatially regulated way.
source: Based on this observation, proper positioning and organization of PCM proteins may be important for promoting different cellular processes in a spatially regulated way (Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citation to Kim et al., 2019.

claim: Aberrations in the function of PCM scaffolds are associated with several human diseases, including cancer and ciliopathies.
source: Not surprisingly, aberrations in the function of PCM scaffolds are associated with several human diseases, including cancer and ciliopathies (Gönczy, 2015; Nigg and Holland, 2018).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations to Gönczy, 2015 and Nigg and Holland, 2018.

claim: CCP110 and CEP97 form a cilia suppressor complex that, when removed from the mother centriole, allows ciliogenesis to proceed.
source: Among them, CCP110 and CEP97 form a cilia suppressor complex that, when removed from the MC, allows ciliogenesis to proceed (Spektor et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citation to Spektor et al., 2007.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton is emerging as key regulator of cilia formation and function, with both negative and positive roles.
source: The actin cytoskeleton is also emerging as key regulator of cilia formation and function, with both negative and positive roles (Copeland, 2020).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citation to Copeland, 2020.

claim: Ciliary dysfunction often results in early developmental problems including hydrocephalus, neural tube closure defects (NTD) and left-right anomalies.
source: Ciliary dysfunction often results in early developmental problems including hydrocephalus, neural tube closure defects (NTD) and left-right anomalies (Fliegauf et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citation to Fliegauf et al., 2007.

claim: Ciliopathies are caused by failure of cilia formation and/or cilia-dependent signaling.
source: These features are often reported in a variety of diseases, collectively known as ciliopathies, caused by failure of cilia formation and/or cilia-dependent signaling (Hildebrandt et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citation to Hildebrandt et al., 2011.

claim: Ciliopathies present a broad spectrum of phenotypes comprising cystic kidneys, polydactyly, obesity or heart malformation.
source: In the adult, depending on the underlying mutation, ciliopathies present a broad spectrum of phenotypes comprising cystic kidneys, polydactyly, obesity or heart malformation.
evidence: This is an explicit list of ciliopathy phenotypes.

claim: LUZP1 was identified by proximity proteomics as an interactor of truncated SALL1.
source: Here we focus on LUZP1, a leucine-zipper motif containing protein that was identified by proximity proteomics as an interactor of truncated SALL1 (Bozal-Basterra et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citation to Bozal-Basterra et al., 2018.

claim: LUZP1 has been previously identified as an interactor of ACTR2 (ARP2 actin related protein two homologue) and filamin A (FLNA).
source: LUZP1 has been previously identified as an interactor of ACTR2 (ARP2 actin related protein two homologue) and filamin A (FLNA) and, recently, as an actin cross-linking protein (Hein et al., 2015; Wang and Nakamura, 2019).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations to Hein et al., 2015 and Wang and Nakamura, 2019.

claim: LUZP1 has been recently identified as an actin cross-linking protein.
source: LUZP1 has been previously identified as an interactor of ACTR2 (ARP2 actin related protein two homologue) and filamin A (FLNA) and, recently, as an actin cross-linking protein (Hein et al., 2015; Wang and Nakamura, 2019).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citation to Wang and Nakamura, 2019.

claim: LUZP1 shows homology to FILIP1, a protein interactor of FLNA and actin.
source: Furthermore, LUZP1 shows homology to FILIP1, a protein interactor of FLNA and actin (Gad et al., 2012; Nagano et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations to Gad et al., 2012 and Nagano et al., 2004.

claim: Mutations in Luzp1 resulted in cardiovascular defects and cranial NTD in mice.
source: Interestingly, mutations in Luzp1 resulted in cardiovascular defects and cranial NTD in mice (Hsu et al., 2008), phenotypes within the spectrum of those seen in TBS individuals and mouse models of dysfunctional cilia (Botzenhart et al., 2007; Botzenhart et al., 2005; Klena et al., 2016; Kohlhase et al., 1998; Surka et al., 2001; Toomer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citation to Hsu et al., 2008.

claim: The phenotypes observed in Luzp1 mutant mice are within the spectrum of those seen in TBS individuals and mouse models of dysfunctional cilia.
source: Interestingly, mutations in Luzp1 resulted in cardiovascular defects and cranial NTD in mice (Hsu et al., 2008), phenotypes within the spectrum of those seen in TBS individuals and mouse models of dysfunctional cilia (Botzenhart et al., 2007; Botzenhart et al., 2005; Klena et al., 2016; Kohlhase et al., 1998; Surka et al., 2001; Toomer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Both the non-canonical Wnt/PCP (Wingless-Integrated/planar cell polarity) and the Shh pathways are influenced by the presence of functional cilia and regulate neural tube closure and patterning.
source: Both the non-canonical Wnt/PCP (Wingless-Integrated/planar cell polarity) and the Shh pathways are influenced by the presence of functional cilia and regulate neural tube closure and patterning (Campbell, 2003; Copp, 2005; Fuccillo et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citations to Campbell, 2003; Copp, 2005; and Fuccillo et al., 2006.

claim: Ectopic Shh was observed in the dorsal lateral neuroepithelium of the Luzp1-/- mice.
source: Remarkably, ectopic Shh was observed in the dorsal lateral neuroepithelium of the Luzp1-/- mice (Hsu et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated and supported by citation to Hsu et al., 2008.

claim: A link between LUZP1 and ciliogenesis has not been explored.
source: However, in spite of the phenotypic overlaps, a link between LUZP1 and ciliogenesis has not been explored.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: LUZP1 is associated with centrosomal and actin cytoskeleton-related proteins.
source: Here we demonstrate that LUZP1 is associated with centrosomal and actin cytoskeleton-related proteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of LUZP1 reduces F-actin levels.
source: Loss of LUZP1 reduces F-actin levels, facilitates ciliogenesis and alters Sonic Hedgehog signaling, pointing to a key role in cytoskeleton-cilia interdependency.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of LUZP1 facilitates ciliogenesis.
source: Loss of LUZP1 reduces F-actin levels, facilitates ciliogenesis and alters Sonic Hedgehog signaling, pointing to a key role in cytoskeleton-cilia interdependency.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of LUZP1 alters Sonic Hedgehog signaling.
source: Loss of LUZP1 reduces F-actin levels, facilitates ciliogenesis and alters Sonic Hedgehog signaling, pointing to a key role in cytoskeleton-cilia interdependency.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: LUZP1 has a key role in cytoskeleton-cilia interdependency.
source: Loss of LUZP1 reduces F-actin levels, facilitates ciliogenesis and alters Sonic Hedgehog signaling, pointing to a key role in cytoskeleton-cilia interdependency.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Truncated SALL1 increases the ubiquitin proteasome-mediated degradation of LUZP1.
source: Truncated SALL1 increases the ubiquitin proteasome-mediated degradation of LUZP1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Alterations in LUZP1 may be contributing to TBS etiology.
source: Together with other factors, alterations in LUZP1 may be contributing to TBS etiology.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: LUZP1 was found among the most enriched proteins in the SALL1275 proximal interactome.
source: LUZP1 was found among the most enriched proteins in the SALL1275 proximal interactome.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and refers to previous proximity proteomics data.

claim: Independent BioID experiments analyzed by western blot using a LUZP1-specific antibody confirmed the interaction between LUZP1 and SALL1275.
source: We confirmed this finding by independent BioID experiments analyzed by western blot using a LUZP1-specific antibody (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Endogenous LUZP1 was able to interact with SALL1275 in pulldown experiments.
source: Our results showed that endogenous LUZP1 was able to interact with SALL1275, confirming our proximity proteomics data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, lane 6, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The interaction of LUZP1 with SALL1275 persisted in presence of overexpressed SALL1FL.
source: The interaction with SALL1275 persisted in presence of overexpressed SALL1FL (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, lane 9, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that heterodimerization of the truncated and FL forms does not inhibit the interaction with LUZP1.
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Heterodimerization of the truncated and FL forms of SALL1 does not inhibit the interaction with LUZP1.
source: The interaction with SALL1275 persisted in presence of overexpressed SALL1FL (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, lane 9, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that heterodimerization of the truncated and FL forms does not inhibit the interaction with LUZP1.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pulldown data.

claim: SALL1FL-YFP also interacts with LUZP1 in pulldown assays when expressed alone.
source: When expressed alone, we noted that SALL1FL-YFP also interacts with LUZP1 in pulldown assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The interaction between SALL1FL and LUZP1 likely occurs in post-lysis cell extracts because these proteins have distinct localizations (nuclear and cytoplasmic, respectively).
source: As these proteins have distinct localizations (nuclear and cytoplasmic, respectively), the interaction likely occurs in post-lysis cell extracts (more in Discussion).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the known subcellular localizations of the proteins.

claim: The truncated form of SALL1 expressed in TBS individuals, either by itself or in complex with the FL form, can interact with LUZP1.
source: These results show that the truncated form of SALL1 expressed in TBS individuals, either by itself or in complex with the FL form, can interact with LUZP1.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the pulldown experiments.

claim: 234 high-confidence proximity LUZP1 interactors were enriched in the TbID-LUZP1 vs the TbID proteome in three replicates.
source: 234 high-confidence proximity LUZP1 interactors were enriched in the TbID-LUZP1 vs the TbID proteome in three replicates (Source Data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the TurboID mass spectrometry experiment.

claim: Proteins enriched among the identified LUZP1 proximal interactors were centrosomal and actin cytoskeleton-related proteins.
source: Proteins enriched among the identified LUZP1 proximal interactors were centrosomal and actin cytoskeleton-related proteins (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the network analysis and volcano plot shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Gene Ontology analysis of LUZP1 proximal interactors showed enrichment in 'actin cytoskeleton', 'microtubule cytoskeleton', 'centrosome', 'cilium' and 'midbody' terms in the Cellular Component domain.
source: In the Cellular Component domain, 'actin cytoskeleton', 'microtubule cytoskeleton', 'centrosome', 'cilium' and 'midbody' terms were highlighted among others (Figure 1D and Source Data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the GO analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: LUZP1 proteome showed enrichment in the 'microtubule cytoskeleton organization', 'cell division', 'cilium assembly', 'vesicle-mediated transport', 'microtubule organizing center organization' and 'cell adhesion' categories in the Biological Process domain.
source: In the category of Biological Process, LUZP1 proteome showed enrichment in the 'microtubule cytoskeleton organization', 'cell division', 'cilium assembly', 'vesicle-mediated transport', 'microtubule organizing center organization' and 'cell adhesion' categories among others (Figure 1D and Source Data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the GO analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: LUZP1 showed enrichment in cytoskeleton-related proteins ('actin binding', 'actinin binding' and 'microtubule binding' terms) in the Molecular Function domain.
source: With respect to Molecular Function, LUZP1 also showed enrichment in cytoskeleton-related proteins ('actin binding', 'actinin binding' and 'microtubule binding' terms; Figure 1D and Source Data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the GO analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 37 verified or 96 potential centrosome/cilia gene products previously identified by proteomic studies were found as LUZP1 proximal interactors.
source: 37 or 96 of the verified or potential, respectively, centrosome/cilia gene products previously identified by proteomic studies (Alves-Cruzeiro et al., 2014; Gupta et al., 2015) were found as LUZP1 proximal interactors, supporting the enrichment of centrosome-related proteins among the potential interactors of LUZP1.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with previously published proteomic datasets.

claim: 45 of LUZP1 proximal interactors were present among the actin-localized proteins identified by the Human Protein Atlas project.
source: In addition, 45 of LUZP1 proximal interactors were present among the actin-localized proteins identified by the Human Protein Atlas project based on subcellular localization to actin filaments (Uhlen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with the Human Protein Atlas database.

claim: Endogenous LUZP1 surrounds both centrioles, labelled by centrin-2 (CETN2) in human RPE1 cells.
source: First, immunostainings showed that endogenous LUZP1 surrounds both centrioles, labelled by centrin-2 (CETN2) in human RPE1 cells (Figure 2A) and gamma-tubulin in human dermal fibroblasts (Figure 2—video 1) (for specificity of LUZP1 antibody, check Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Endogenous LUZP1 surrounds both centrioles, labelled by gamma-tubulin in human dermal fibroblasts.
source: First, immunostainings showed that endogenous LUZP1 surrounds both centrioles, labelled by centrin-2 (CETN2) in human RPE1 cells (Figure 2A) and gamma-tubulin in human dermal fibroblasts (Figure 2—video 1) (for specificity of LUZP1 antibody, check Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—video 1.

claim: LUZP1 was reduced at the centrosome during G2/M and G0 phases.
source: LUZP1 was reduced at the centrosome during G2/M and G0 phases (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in synchronized cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: LUZP1 levels increased upon treatment with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 in G0 phase arrested-RPE1 cells.
source: Interestingly, LUZP1 levels increased upon treatment with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 in G0 phase arrested-RPE1 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: LUZP1 levels are reduced at the centrosome in G2/M phase and upon starvation, and this reduction might be mediated by the UPS.
source: All together, these results indicate that LUZP1 levels are reduced at the centrosome in G2/M phase and upon starvation, and this reduction might be mediated by the UPS.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cell cycle and MG132 treatment data.

claim: LUZP1-YFP does not colocalize with the distal centriolar marker CCP110.
source: We did not observe colocalization of LUZP1 with the distal centriolar marker CCP110 (Figure 2B), indicating that LUZP1 is likely found at the proximal end of both centrioles.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: LUZP1 is likely found at the proximal end of both centrioles.
source: We did not observe colocalization of LUZP1 with the distal centriolar marker CCP110 (Figure 2B), indicating that LUZP1 is likely found at the proximal end of both centrioles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of colocalization with CCP110.

claim: LUZP1 enveloped PCNT (pericentrin).
source: Interestingly, we observed that LUZP1 enveloped PCNT (Figure 2C), with LUZP1 itself being surrounded by PCM1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: LUZP1 is surrounded by PCM1.
source: Interestingly, we observed that LUZP1 enveloped PCNT (Figure 2C), with LUZP1 itself being surrounded by PCM1 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: LUZP1 might be a novel PCM associated-protein, decorating the proximal end of both centrioles.
source: These results suggest that LUZP1 might be a novel PCM associated-protein, decorating the proximal end of both centrioles.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the localization data relative to PCNT and PCM1.

claim: LUZP1 was associated to PCM1 in TurboID experiments.
source: In concordance with this localization, LUZP1 was associated to PCM1 in TurboID experiments (Source Data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the TurboID mass spectrometry data.

claim: LUZP1 localizes to actin stress fibers in U2OS cells.
source: In addition to the localization at the centrosome/basal body, LUZP1 also localized to actin stress fibers (Figure 2E) and to the midbody (Figure 2F) in U2OS cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: LUZP1 localizes to the midbody in U2OS cells.
source: In addition to the localization at the centrosome/basal body, LUZP1 also localized to actin stress fibers (Figure 2E) and to the midbody (Figure 2F) in U2OS cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: LUZP1 was markedly decreased at the centrosome of TBS275 cells compared to control cells in non-starved conditions.
source: We observed that LUZP1 was markedly decreased at the centrosome of TBS275 cells compared to control cells in non-starved conditions (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: LUZP1 levels decreased in starved vs non-starved control cells.
source: Furthermore, LUZP1 levels decreased in starved vs non-starved control cells (Figure 3A–C), while centrosomal size remained unaltered (Figure 3C, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Centrosomal size remained unaltered in starved vs non-starved control cells.
source: Furthermore, LUZP1 levels decreased in starved vs non-starved control cells (Figure 3A–C), while centrosomal size remained unaltered (Figure 3C, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: LUZP1-YFP interacts with CCP110 and CEP97 in both WT (293WT) and TBS model (293335) HEK 293FT cells.
source: Indeed, LUZP1-YFP interacts with CCP110 and CEP97 in both WT (293WT) and TBS model (293335) HEK 293FT cells (Figure 3D, lanes 5 and 7, respectively and Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Bozal-Basterra et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Less CCP110 and CEP97 was recovered in LUZP1-YFP pulldowns from 293335 cells, likely due to the reduced LUZP1-YFP seen in those cells.
source: Less CCP110 and CEP97 was recovered in LUZP1-YFP pulldowns from 293335 cells, but this is likely due to the reduced LUZP1-YFP seen in those cells (Figure 3D, Input, lanes 1 and 2 vs lane 3 and 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pulldown data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of endogenous LUZP1 led to co-purification of endogenous CCP110.
source: Beyond pulldowns, we found that immunoprecipitation of endogenous LUZP1 led to co-purification of endogenous CCP110 (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and that anti-CEP97 antibodies immunoprecipitated endogenous LUZP1 (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Anti-CEP97 antibodies immunoprecipitated endogenous LUZP1.
source: Beyond pulldowns, we found that immunoprecipitation of endogenous LUZP1 led to co-purification of endogenous CCP110 (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and that anti-CEP97 antibodies immunoprecipitated endogenous LUZP1 (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Both CCP110 and CEP97 were identified as proximal interactors of TbID-LUZP1.
source: Both CCP110 and CEP97 were also identified as proximal interactors of TbID-LUZP1 (Source Data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the TurboID mass spectrometry data.

claim: Immunofluorescent colocalization on centrioles of LUZP1 (proximal) and CCP110 (distal) was not evident.
source: Immunofluorescent colocalization on centrioles of LUZP1 (proximal) and CCP110 (distal) was not evident, suggesting that the interaction is indirect or occurs before proteins reach their destinations.
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence experiments.

claim: The interaction between LUZP1 and CCP110 is indirect or occurs before proteins reach their destinations.
source: Immunofluorescent colocalization on centrioles of LUZP1 (proximal) and CCP110 (distal) was not evident, suggesting that the interaction is indirect or occurs before proteins reach their destinations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the lack of colocalization despite biochemical interaction.

claim: A reduction in both actin-associated LUZP1 and phalloidin-labelled stress fibers was observed in TBS275 cells when compared to control cells.
source: Intriguingly, when LUZP1 levels were examined in TBS275 cells, a reduction in both actin-associated LUZP1 and phalloidin-labelled stress fibers was observed when compared to control cells (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Actin cytoskeleton might be altered in TBS cells.
source: These results indicate that actin cytoskeleton might be altered in TBS cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the reduced F-actin observed in TBS275 cells.

claim: LUZP1-YFP interacts with both actin and FLNA in pulldown assays.
source: Using pulldown assays, we confirmed that LUZP1-YFP interacts with both actin and FLNA (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by pulldown data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Actin, FLNA, alpha-actinin, palladin, LIMA1/Eplin and other stress fiber-associated proteins are proximal interactors of TbID-LUZP1.
source: Notably, actin, FLNA, alpha-actinin, palladin, LIMA1/Eplin and other stress fiber-associated proteins are proximal interactors of TbID-LUZP1 (Source Data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the TurboID mass spectrometry data.

claim: No changes in LUZP1 levels upon actin depolymerization were observed when cells were lysed in strong lysis conditions (WB5).
source: No changes in LUZP1 levels upon actin depolymerization were observed when cells were lysed in strong lysis conditions (WB5) (Figure 4E–F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Increased LUZP1 levels were observed using mild lysis conditions (0.1% Triton X-100) upon actin depolymerization.
source: However, we observed increased LUZP1 levels using mild lysis conditions (0.1% Triton X-100; Figure 4E–F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: The integrity of the actin cytoskeleton may influence the solubility but not the stability of LUZP1.
source: These results reflect that the integrity of the actin cytoskeleton may influence the solubility but not the stability of LUZP1.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differential effects of lysis conditions on LUZP1 detection after CytoD treatment.

claim: Luzp1-/- fibroblasts displayed higher ciliation rate (60%) than WT (10.5%) and +LUZP1 (22.2%) when the cells were not subjected to starvation.

evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the overexpression and CytoD experiments.

claim: LUZP1 might be a contributing factor to the TBS phenotype via its interaction with truncated SALL1 and its effect on ciliogenesis.
source: We conclude that LUZP1 might be a contributing factor to the TBS phenotype via its interaction with truncated SALL1 and its effect on ciliogenesis, based on several findings: i) LUZP1 levels are reduced in TBS-derived cells likely due to truncated SALL1-mediated degradation through the UPS; ii) LUZP1 interacts with proteins of the centrosome and of the actin cytoskeleton; iii) In the absence of LUZP1, the assembly and growth of primary cilia is enhanced in cycling cells, accompanied by an increase in basal Shh signaling, and the actin cytoskeleton is reduced; iv) Increase of LUZP1 reduces the levels of ciliogenesis in TBS-individuals derived cells.
